Glossary

    Examples · Pro

    Words: 1090

    Seven techniques for the “my scripts run on other people's machines” level. The goal of this level is to eliminate silent failures: whatever can go wrong must report it out loud.

    Key idea of this page #

    The difference between Noob and Pro is not command recall, but the approach to failure. A beginner scripts the happy path; a professional assumes commands will fail, network connections will flap, and the script will be executed twice concurrently or interrupted mid-run. The seven techniques below target precisely these realities: loud failures with line numbers, guaranteed temporary file cleanup, non-destructive dry-run modes, bounded retries, bounded concurrency with error aggregation, single-instance execution locks, and logging that does not pollute data streams. None of them are complex. What is difficult is remembering them before an incident occurs, rather than after.

    1 · Failing loudly: trap ERR with line numbers #

    Task: Ensure a failing script automatically reports where the failure occurred.

    #!/usr/bin/env bash
set -Eeuo pipefail

on_err() {
  local rc=$?
  echo "FAILURE: line $1, exit code $rc" >&2
  exit "$rc"
}
trap 'on_err $LINENO' ERR
    Why this works: Bash lacks stack traces on failure, so the failure line number is the sole substitute for a trace. The -E option is mandatory: without it, the ERR trap is not inherited by shell functions or subshells, causing errors inside functions to bypass the handler. local rc=$? must be captured on the very first line: any subsequent command overwrites the exit status.

    2 · Temporary directory guaranteed to clean up #

    Task: Process intermediate files leaving zero debris on error or Ctrl+C.

    tmp=$(mktemp -d "${TMPDIR:-/tmp}/app.XXXXXX")
cleanup() { rm -rf "$tmp"; }
trap cleanup EXIT INT TERM

work > "$tmp/out"
mv "$tmp/out" result.txt
    Why this works: The EXIT pseudo-signal trap runs on any script termination, including set -e failures - with the sole exception of SIGKILL, which the kernel prohibits trapping. INT and TERM add handling for terminal interruptions and process termination signals. Let mktemp generate unique names: predictable filenames in shared /tmp create race conditions under concurrent runs and open symlink attack vulnerabilities. Atomic renaming into final placement ensures callers never observe a partially written file.

    3 · Command options and mandatory --dry-run #

    Task: Equip a script with options and a “show what would happen without executing” mode.

    dry=0; verbose=0
while getopts ":nvh" opt; do
  case $opt in
    n) dry=1 ;;
    v) verbose=1 ;;
    h) usage; exit 0 ;;
    \?) echo "unknown option" >&2; exit 2 ;;
  esac
done
shift $((OPTIND - 1))

run() { (( dry )) && { echo "DRY: $*"; return 0; }; "$@"; }
run rm -rf "$target"
    Why this works: A leading colon in the option specification string puts getopts into silent mode, giving you control over error reporting. shift $((OPTIND - 1)) consumes parsed options, leaving $1 pointing to the first positional argument. The run wrapper makes dry-run support architectural rather than an afterthought: all mutating commands pass through it, making omitting --dry-run harder than remembering it. One critical caveat: shell redirections are evaluated before entering a function. run echo x > file truncates file even in dry-run mode because > has already executed. Encapsulate file writing inside the command: run sh -c 'echo x > file' or write through a dedicated helper function that performs its own dry-run check.

    4 · Retries with exponential backoff #

    Task: Survive transient network hiccups without degenerating into an infinite loop.

    retry() {
  local n=0 max=5 delay=1
  until "$@"; do
    n=$((n + 1))
    (( n >= max )) && return 1
    sleep "$delay"
    delay=$((delay * 2))
  done
}

retry curl -fsS --max-time 10 "$url"
    Why this works: Three conditions distinguish a resilient retry from an infinite hang: an attempt ceiling, growing backoff delays, and a command-level timeout. Without --max-time, retries are useless: the very first request can stall indefinitely. curl -f is mandatory: without it, HTTP 500 errors are treated as successful exits, leaving nothing to retry.

    5 · Bounded parallel processing with error aggregation #

    Task: Process a hundred files across four parallel workers and verify if any failed.

    export -f process          # visible in xargs

printf '%s\0' logs/*.log \
  | xargs -0 -P4 -I{} bash -c 'process "$@"' _ {} \
  || echo "some tasks failed" >&2

# manual tracking with exit codes:
pids=(); for f in logs/*.log; do work "$f" & pids+=($!); done
rc=0; for p in "${pids[@]}"; do wait "$p" || rc=1; done
    Why this works: The null delimiter \0 paired with -0 immunizes the pipeline against filenames with spaces and newlines. xargs returns a non-zero exit status if any sub-process fails - providing the aggregated error detection absent in naive & plus wait workflows. If you need individual process exit codes, store $! in an array and wait on each PID individually.

    6 · Single instance: protecting against concurrent runs #

    Task: Prevent a cron job from starting a second instance if the previous run is still active.

    exec 9>/var/lock/app.lock
flock -n 9 || { echo "already running" >&2; exit 0; }

# subsequent standard execution
    Why this works: The lock is bound to an open file descriptor, not a filesystem path: it is released automatically when the process terminates - including abrupt crashes. A custom “pid-file / flag-file” lacks this property: upon an unhandled crash, stale lock files remain on disk blocking future runs permanently. The -n flag requests non-blocking acquisition; exiting with status 0 is deliberate here - for cron, an already running instance is an expected condition, not a failure.

    7 · Leveled logging #

    Task: Provide diagnostic logging that does not corrupt command stdout.

    LOG_LEVEL="${LOG_LEVEL:-info}"
_log() {
  local lvl=$1; shift
  printf '%s [%s] %s\n' \
    "$(date -Is)" "$lvl" "$*" >&2
}
info() { [ "$LOG_LEVEL" = debug ] || [ "$LOG_LEVEL" = info ] && _log INFO "$@"; }
die()  { _log ERROR "$@"; exit 1; }
    Why this works: All log output is directed to stderr because stdout is reserved for data consumed by downstream pipeline stages. Timestamps formatted with -Is (ISO 8601) sort naturally as strings and parse unambiguously by machine tools. Log level is driven by an environment variable: verbosity can be toggled without editing script code - essential when triaging issues in production.

    Artifacts: what you take away from this page #

    Reading >> Your life quantum · Dignity partnership with AI · Rewiring your neural network

    Seven modular patterns and the exact failures each defends against. Your time was well spent if when drafting your next script you reflexively ask “what happens if this crashes midway through” - and already know the solution. That is the essence of rewiring: failure handling stops being an afterthought and becomes an integral part of design.

    1. set -Eeuo pipefail and trap ERR $LINENO - failures name their exact location.
    2. mktemp -d with trap EXIT INT TERM - guaranteed cleanup on all exits except kill -9.
    3. getopts and the run wrapper - architectural dry-run checks and internal redirection.
    4. Bounded retries with timeouts, and why curl -f is mandatory.
    5. xargs -0 -P - safe filenames and aggregated exit status reporting.
    6. Descriptor-based flock instead of brittle pid-files.
    7. Stderr logging with environment-driven log levels.
